scenes.visual: Title card 'Stopping Partway' fades in over the same round cartoon cell as the first film, with its OLIVE-GREEN mitochondrion. Same world and COLOUR MAP as the first film: GLUCOSE = SAND six-segment block; ATP = GOLD token with three beads; ADP = GOLD token with two beads; OXYGEN = BLUE dots; CARBON DIOXIDE = GREY puffs; WATER = PALE-AQUA drops; MITOCHONDRION = OLIVE-GREEN bean with a wavy fold; LACTATE and ETHANOL = ORANGE halves. COUNTER top right: 'ATP rebuilt from this glucose: n'. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Can a cell still rebuild A T P when oxygen-using respiration can't keep up? A sprinting leg and yeast sealed in dough both face this problem.
scenes.caption: Can a cell still rebuild ATP when oxygen-using respiration can't keep up? A sprinting leg and yeast sealed in dough both face this problem.
scenes.visual: Split screen: a sprinter's leg pumping hard on the left, a ball of dough wrapped in plastic on the right. Above each, a BLUE oxygen tap drips slowly. Question card: 'ATP without enough oxygen?'
scenes.narration: Can a cell still rebuild ATP when oxygen-using respiration can't keep up? A sprinting leg and yeast sealed in dough both face this problem.

scenes.tts: In the first film, glucose began breaking down in the cytoplasm. With oxygen, the mitochondrion finished the job. That gave about thirty A T P per glucose. Now we turn the oxygen down and watch the same cell.
scenes.caption: In the first film, glucose began breaking down in the cytoplasm. With oxygen, the mitochondrion finished the job. That gave about thirty ATP per glucose. Now we turn the oxygen down and watch the same cell.
scenes.visual: A quick replay strip of the first film's ending: BLUE dots flowing in, the COUNTER at 'about 30'. Then the strip fades and the live cell returns. A hand turns the BLUE oxygen tap down; the BLUE dots in the cell thin out and fade. The COUNTER resets to 0.
scenes.narration: In the first film, glucose began breaking down in the cytoplasm. With oxygen, the mitochondrion finished the job. That gave about thirty ATP per glucose. Now we turn the oxygen down and watch the same cell.

scenes.tts: The first steps still run in the cytoplasm. They need no oxygen, and they are the same steps as before. Glucose splits in two, and the counter reaches two A T P.
scenes.caption: The first steps still run in the cytoplasm. They need no oxygen, and they are the same steps as before. Glucose splits in two, and the counter reaches two ATP.
scenes.visual: A SAND six-segment block drifts into the cytoplasm and splits into two halves, exactly as in the first film. Two ADP tokens nearby get their third bead clicked back. The COUNTER ticks to 2 and holds there, highlighted. Label beside the split: 'same first steps, no oxygen needed'.
scenes.narration: The first steps still run in the cytoplasm. They need no oxygen, and they are the same steps as before. Glucose splits in two, and the counter reaches two ATP.

scenes.tts: With too little oxygen, or too much demand, the mitochondrion can't keep up. Some halves can't go on into it. For those, the cell has to stop partway. Their energy stays locked inside.
scenes.visual: More SAND halves arrive than the OLIVE-GREEN mitochondrion can take. A few halves still trickle in through its entrance, slowly, as the thin BLUE dots allow; the rest bump off and wait in the cytoplasm, labelled 'stops partway'. The dotted 'all the way down' path into the mitochondrion carries only a thin trickle.
scenes.caption: With too little oxygen, or too much demand, the mitochondrion can't keep up. Some halves can't go on into it. For those, the cell has to stop partway. Their energy stays locked inside.
scenes.narration: With too little oxygen, or too much demand, the mitochondrion can't keep up. Some halves can't go on into it. For those, the cell has to stop partway. Their energy stays locked inside.

scenes.tts: In a working muscle cell, the halves become lactate. Lactate builds up when the muscle makes it faster than it can be used. Your leg muscles do this during a hard sprint.
scenes.visual: Left panel, a muscle fibre: the two SAND halves turn ORANGE and are labelled 'lactate'. More glucose blocks arrive and split, and ORANGE lactate halves pile up inside the fibre, faster than a slow trickle leaves through the fibre's edge.
scenes.caption: In a working muscle cell, the halves become lactate. Lactate builds up when the muscle makes it faster than it can be used. Your leg muscles do this during a hard sprint.
scenes.narration: In a working muscle cell, the halves become lactate. Lactate builds up when the muscle makes it faster than it can be used. Your leg muscles do this during a hard sprint.

scenes.tts: In yeast, the halves become ethanol and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide forms the bubbles that make bread dough rise.
scenes.visual: Right panel, a cartoon yeast cell inside the dough: the halves turn into ORANGE pieces labelled 'ethanol' plus GREY puffs labelled 'carbon dioxide'. The GREY puffs gather into bubbles in the dough, and the dough ball swells under its plastic wrap.
scenes.caption: In yeast, the halves become ethanol and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide forms the bubbles that make bread dough rise.
scenes.narration: In yeast, the halves become ethanol and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide forms the bubbles that make bread dough rise.

scenes.tts: This partway route has a name. Biologists call it fermentation. It runs in the cytoplasm and never uses the mitochondrion. Watch the counter. Turning the halves into lactate or ethanol adds nothing. Both A T P came from the first steps.
scenes.visual: Both panels shrink side by side under one banner: 'fermentation'. A dotted outline traces the route, glucose to halves to ORANGE leftovers, all inside the cytoplasm. The OLIVE-GREEN mitochondrion is not part of this route and is dimmed. The COUNTER stays at 2 while the halves turn ORANGE; a small '+0' flashes beside it.
scenes.caption: This partway route has a name. Biologists call it fermentation. It runs in the cytoplasm and never uses the mitochondrion. Watch the counter. Turning the halves into lactate or ethanol adds nothing. Both ATP came from the first steps.
scenes.narration: This partway route has a name. Biologists call it fermentation. It runs in the cytoplasm and never uses the mitochondrion. Watch the counter. Turning the halves into lactate or ethanol adds nothing. Both ATP came from the first steps.

scenes.tts: Why only two A T P? Look at the leftovers. Lactate and ethanol still hold over nine tenths of the energy that was in the glucose. Fermentation frees only a small part of it.
scenes.caption: Why only two ATP? Look at the leftovers. Lactate and ethanol still hold over nine-tenths of the energy that was in the glucose. Fermentation frees only a small part of it.
scenes.visual: A tall energy bar appears beside one SAND glucose block, labelled 'energy in one glucose'. An identical bar appears beside the ORANGE lactate leftovers and beside the ORANGE ethanol leftovers; each stays filled to above a dashed line marked 'nine-tenths'. Only a thin top slice of each bar is coloured GOLD, labelled 'freed: small part'. Caption under the bars: 'over 90 % left in the leftovers (schematic)'.
scenes.narration: Why only two ATP? Look at the leftovers. Lactate and ethanol still hold over nine-tenths of the energy that was in the glucose. Fermentation frees only a small part of it.

scenes.tts: So suppose a cell needs thirty A T P, and it has no oxygen. How many glucose must it break down?
scenes.caption: So suppose a cell needs thirty ATP, and it has no oxygen. How many glucose must it break down?
scenes.visual: A target badge appears: 'ATP needed: 30'. Two cells side by side: left labelled 'with oxygen', right labelled 'fermentation'. Question card: 'How many glucose for 30 ATP by fermentation?'
scenes.narration: So suppose a cell needs thirty ATP, and it has no oxygen. How many glucose must it break down?

scenes.visual: Hold on the two cells and the question card. A thin timer bar runs across the bottom.

scenes.tts: Fifteen glucose. With oxygen, about one would do. Without it, the fermenting cell has to pull in glucose after glucose just to keep up. That is about fifteen times as much glucose for the same A T P.
scenes.visual: Race: in the left cell one SAND block enters, goes all the way down, and its counter fills to 30. In the right cell SAND blocks enter one after another, each adding 2; a tally reads 1, 2, 3 ... 15 glucose. On-screen working: '30 ATP ÷ 2 ATP per glucose = 15 glucose'. The right cell's ORANGE leftovers pile high.
scenes.caption: Fifteen glucose. With oxygen, about one would do. Without it, the fermenting cell has to pull in glucose after glucose just to keep up. That is about fifteen times as much glucose for the same ATP.
scenes.narration: Fifteen glucose. With oxygen, about one would do. Without it, the fermenting cell has to pull in glucose after glucose just to keep up. That is about fifteen times as much glucose for the same ATP.

scenes.tts: Fermentation does have strengths. It needs no oxygen, and it can make A T P quickly. So a hard-working muscle adds it when oxygen-using respiration can't keep up. The mitochondria keep working too. Yeast in sealed dough has no other choice.
scenes.caption: Fermentation does have strengths. It needs no oxygen, and it can make ATP quickly. So a hard-working muscle adds it when oxygen-using respiration can't keep up. The mitochondria keep working too. Yeast in sealed dough has no other choice.
scenes.visual: The sprinter's leg returns. Two GOLD supply lines feed it: a thick steady one from the mitochondrion labelled 'with oxygen' and a fast thin one from the cytoplasm labelled 'fermentation'. As the leg speeds up, the fermentation line switches on beside the first one, and the mitochondrion line keeps flowing.
scenes.narration: Fermentation does have strengths. It needs no oxygen, and it can make ATP quickly. So a hard-working muscle adds it when oxygen-using respiration can't keep up. The mitochondria keep working too. Yeast in sealed dough has no other choice.

scenes.tts: Take a glucose all the way apart, and the cell rebuilds about thirty A T P. Stop it partway, and it rebuilds two. Most of the energy stays behind in the leftovers. Same glucose, same first steps, very different payoff.
scenes.caption: Take a glucose all the way apart, and the cell rebuilds about thirty ATP. Stop it partway, and it rebuilds two. Most of the energy stays behind in the leftovers. Same glucose, same first steps, very different payoff.
scenes.visual: Two rows, like a ladder. Top row: SAND block → halves → mitochondrion → GREY puffs and PALE-AQUA drops; COUNTER 'about 30'. Bottom row: SAND block → halves → ORANGE lactate or ethanol; COUNTER '2', with the ORANGE leftovers still glowing with a nearly full energy bar.
scenes.narration: Take a glucose all the way apart, and the cell rebuilds about thirty ATP. Stop it partway, and it rebuilds two. Most of the energy stays behind in the leftovers. Same glucose, same first steps, very different payoff.

scenes.visual: End card with the logo hexagon character. Take-home line: 'How far each glucose is taken apart sets how much ATP returns.'
